clips.why: Why frontier LLMs fall short at workflow automation. Hook: 'one area that always felt short ... was workflow automation' (the next line's 'here' needs it, so no later start). Payoff lands at 81.8: TypeSafe's claim that optimizing for human preference and verifiable reward doesn't carry over to quick decisions under uncertainty. Ending at 108.7 (after 'forcing a chat/agent model into automation is fundamentally wrong') also works, restating it more bluntly; hence the wide end range.

Hot take: the Jev demos show off speed, not depth of understanding. LLMs can functionally do the same tasks but can't hit 70-500ms because autoregressive decoding is sequential; Jev is built for parallel sampling and typed probabilistic decisions (162.3). 154.3 already lands the latency point; 176.6 adds a 'so it's less about...' summary.

Explains how using Jev differs from an LLM: structured in, probability distribution out, 'okay, what do I do with this?', the three primitives (choice, score, yes/no), payoff on 'it feels like we're back to logic gates and registers' (308.8). One 'looks something like this' screen reference, but the point is spoken.

Closing opinion: the news is about use cases growing horizontally, not Jev's novelty; narrow specialized models predate generative AI, and it's healthy to stop brute-forcing one foundation model for every task. Opening at 374.3 (TypeSafe hasn't disclosed RLCD; someone on Reddit built a similar 421M BERT model) adds the evidence for 'not novel' and is also acceptable; 393.8 is the tighter hook.
